text: Newton's second law for rotation. Defining Newton's second law for rotation in vector form. Since torque is a rotational analog to force, is there an analogous equation to Newton's second law? Let's start with Newton's second law for a single particle rotating around an axis in circular motion. A force vector f is applied on a point mass m that is a distance r from a pivot point. See the figure? The particle is constrained to move in a circular path with a fixed radius and the force is tangent to the path. We apply Newton's second law to determine the magnitude of the acceleration, a equals f over m in the direction of vector f. Since the force is tangential to the path, we can use the relation for the tangential acceleration that relates to the angular acceleration, a equals r alpha. Substituting this expression into Newton's second law, we have f equals mA equals mR alpha. We can multiply both sides by the radius r, which is motivated by the form of the torque, tau equals rF sin theta. The force is applied perpendicular to r, thus sin theta equals 1. Now we have rF equals mR squared alpha. tau equals mR squared alpha equals i alpha. If we substitute the moment of inertia i equals mR squared, then we have a form that is similar to Newton's second law. In this form, the torque plays the role of force. The moment of inertia is like mass and the angular acceleration is the rotational analog to the translational acceleration. Newton's second law for rotation. If more than one torque acts on a rigid body about a fixed axis, then the sum of the torques equals the moment of inertia times the angular acceleration. tau net equals sum sub j tau j equals i alpha. The term i alpha is a scalar quantity that can be positive counterclockwise or negative clockwise, depending on the sign of the net torque. This relation is Newton's second law for rotation and tells us how to analyze problems for rotational dynamics. Deriving Newton's second law for rotation in vector form. Newton's second law tells us the relationship between the net force and how to change the translational motion of an object. We have a vector rotational equivalent of this equation. Let's start with the tangential acceleration written as a cross product. Vector A equals vector alpha times vector R. We form the cross product of this equation with vector R because we are ultimately wanting to generate a relation for vector tau equals vector R times vector F. Note that you might want to review the vector algebra section from chapter two. We begin with vector R times vector A equals vector R times vector alpha times vector R equals vector alpha, vector R dot vector R equals R squared vector alpha. We use the vector triple product to resolve the cross product of a cross product. Since vector R is perpendicular to vector alpha, this means that the dot product vector R dot vector alpha equals zero. In Newton's second law, the mass M acts as a scalar on the acceleration vector A. Applying that here, we have vector F equals some M vector A. Vector tau equals some vector R times vector F equals vector R times M vector A. Equals M vector R times vector A equals M R squared vector alpha. Since I equals M R squared, we arrive at Newton's second law of rotation in vector form. tau net equals some vector tau equals I vector alpha. Note that the torque vector is in the same direction as the angular acceleration. Applying Newton's second law for rotation, problem solving strategy, rotational dynamics. First, identify that torque and mass are involved in the rotation. Second, determine the system of interest. Third, draw a free body diagram for each system of interest. Fourth, identify the pivot points. Choose the pivot point that simplifies your work the most. Fifth, apply some sub J tau J equals I alpha to solve the problem. Carefully select the moment of inertia and consider the torque about the point of rotation. Sixth, check the solution for physical reasonableness. Example problem, effect of mass distribution on a merry-go-round. The problem, consider the father pushing a playground merry-go-round in figure. He exerts a force of 250 newtons at the edge of the 50 kilogram merry-go-round, which has a 1.5-0 meters radius. Calculate the angular acceleration produced for part A when no one is on the merry-go-round, and for part B when an 18 kilogram child sits 1.25 meters away from the center. Consider the merry-go-round itself to be a uniform disc with negligible friction. The worked solution follows. The model. The merry-go-round rotates about a fixed central axis. The applied force is perpendicular to the radius, so it produces the maximum possible torque for the given force and radius. Because friction is negligible, the applied torque is the net torque on the system. The angular acceleration follows from Newton's second law for rotation. The applied torque is the same in both cases, but the moment of inertia changes when the child is added. The merry-go-round is modeled as a uniform disc, and the child is modeled as a point mass located at a fixed distance from the axis. The math. The applied force is perpendicular to the radius, so the torque magnitude is determined by the force and radius. The applied torque follows from the given radius and force. Tao equals 1.50 meters times 250 Nt, equals 375 Nt. meter. For part A, the merry-go-round is modeled as a uniform disc, so its moment of inertia is i equals 1.5 mR squared. equals 1.5 times 50 kg times 1.50 meters squared. equals 56.25 kg dot square meters. Newton's second law for rotation relates the net torque, moment of inertia, and angular acceleration. We solve this relationship for the angular acceleration, which gives alpha equals Tao over i. The angular acceleration follows from the applied torque and the moment of inertia. Alpha equals 375 Nt. meter over 56.25 kg dot square meters. equals 6.67 radians per second squared. For part B, the child is modeled as a point mass, so the child's moment of inertia is i equals mR squared. i sub c equals mR squared. The child's moment of inertia follows from the child's mass and distance from the axis. i sub c equals 18 kg times 1.25 meters squared. equals 28.13 kg dot meters squared. The total moment of inertia of the system is the sum of the merry-go-round and child contributions. i total equals 56.25 kg dot meter squared. plus 28.13 kg dot meter squared. equals 84.38 kg dot meter squared. The same rotational form of Newton's second law applies after the child is added. We solve this relationship for the angular acceleration, which gives alpha equals Tao over i total. The angular acceleration follows from the same applied torque and the larger moment of inertia. Alpha equals 375 Nt. meters over 84.38 kg dot meter squared. equals 4.44 radians per second squared. The conclusion. When the merry-go-round is empty, the angular acceleration is 6.67 radians per second squared. When the 18 kg child sits 1.25 meters from the center, the angular acceleration decreases to 4.4 radians per second squared. This result shows that increasing the mass farther from the axis increases the moment of inertia and reduces the angular acceleration produced by the same torque. The change in mass distribution matters just as much as the total mass when rotational motion is involved.
